item.title: Raye Tops the 2027 Grammy Nominations With 11 Including Album of the Year
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Leading the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11 nods, Raye picks up Album of the Year for This Music May Contain Hope and Record and Song of the Year for "WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!" alongside her emotional online reaction.

The post Raye Tops the 2027 Grammy Nominations With 11 Including Album of the Year appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Raye singing on stage with her band and backing vocalists. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram 

When the 2027 Grammy nominations dropped earlier this week, one name sat right at the top of the entire board: Raye. Out of every artist in the running for the 69th Annual Grammy Awards, she has the highest Grammy nominations this year with 11 nods, putting her ahead of Rosalía on nine.

If you have been watching her rise over the past few years, seeing her command this much spotlight on music’s biggest stage feels well earned, especially for readers following global talent with Ghanaian roots through her mother’s side of the family. Her reaction online captured just how surreal the moment felt, writing on Instagram: “WHAT IS HAPPENING WHAT IS HAPPENING 11 GRAMMY NOMINATIONS INCLUDING ALBUM OF THE YEAR MY HEARTTTTT CANNOT EVEN FATHOM, MY HEARTTTTTTTT ” before following up with a simple “can’t stop crying .”

Raye at home with her parents following the 2027 Grammy nominations announcement. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram 

In case you are still catching up on her story, Raye was born Rachel Keen in London to a Ghanaian-Swiss mother and an English father, and she has spent years building a reputation as a sharp songwriter, vocalist, and arranger who refuses to stay boxed into one sound.

Many listeners first got to know her through chart-topping collaborations and pop hooks before she parted ways with her former major label to release music independently, taking full creative control of her catalogue and storytelling. That independent leap paid off massively—her album This Music May Contain Hope topped the UK chart in March 2026 and won the 2026 Mercury Prize in October, turning her into one of the most talked-about voices in music.

Artwork for This Music May Contain Hope. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram 

Her 11 nominations for 2027 stretch right across her artistry, from songwriting and performance to arrangement, visuals, and full-length projects. This Music May Contain Hope is competing in both Album of the Year and Best Pop Vocal Album, while her hit “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!“—which reached UK No. 1 in January 2026—is up for Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Pop Solo Performance.

She also earned nods for “Click Clack Symphony” alongside Hans Zimmer in Best Pop Duo/Group Performance, Best Arrangement, Instrumental and Vocals, and Best Music Video, plus “Life Boat” in Best Dance Pop Recording, “I Hate the Way I Look Today” in Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance, and a Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical nod.

Raye holding a number one award following a year of UK chart milestones, including “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!” hitting No. 1 in January 2026 and This Music May Contain Hope topping the UK chart in March 2026. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram 

This is not her first time on the Grammy radar, though it is easily her biggest moment yet. Before this sweep, Raye had four prior Grammy nominations—taking her career total to 15—including Best New Artist, Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical, and Best Engineered Album, Non-Classical in 2025, plus Best Music Film in 2026 for Live at the Royal Albert Hall.

While the Recording Academy previously honoured her with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte Best Song for Social Change Award for her songwriting on “Ice Cream Man“, she has never won a competitive Grammy. With 11 chances coming up at the 2027 ceremony on February 7, 2027, we will all be watching to see if she finally brings home her first competitive win—or a whole shelf of them.

Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11 nods across categories including Album of the Year, Record of the Year, and Song of the Year. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram

item.title: A Safari, a Beach & Easy Entry? 5 African Spots for Your Christmas Holiday
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Five African destinations—Kenya, Rwanda, Mauritius, Ghana, and Côte d'Ivoire—give Nigerian travellers easy entry for a Christmas holiday, mixing wildlife safaris, beach escapes, city dining, and full itineraries.

The post A Safari, a Beach & Easy Entry? 5 African Spots for Your Christmas Holiday appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Five African destinations Nigerian passport holders can visit visa-free or with visa on arrival this Christmas holiday. Image: AI-generated.

The group chat has the concerts, the dinners and the Detty December link-ups covered. But has anyone planned the getaway? Beyond the usual Lagos parties and end-of-year outings, there is a whole continent waiting to be explored, with sun-soaked beaches, wildlife safaris, exciting food scenes and cities with plenty of stories to tell.

You do not have to spend weeks navigating embassy appointments and visa applications to make it happen, either. Several African countries offer Nigerian passport holders visa-free entry or visas on arrival, making a festive-season escape much easier to plan. Whether you are travelling solo, gathering your friends, taking the family along or joining a curated travel group, here are five destinations worth considering for your Christmas holiday.

Kenya

Imagine spotting lions and giraffes against a city skyline before breakfast, then catching an evening flight or train straight to the coast for fresh seafood by the Indian Ocean. That contrast is what makes Kenya such a rewarding December escape. Nairobi gives you immediate access to wildlife at Nairobi National Park and the Giraffe Centre alongside lively restaurants and art spaces in Westlands and Karen, while longer itineraries open up classic game drives in the Maasai Mara, views of Mount Kilimanjaro in Amboseli, and warm beach days in Diani or Watamu. Nigerian citizens enjoy visa-free entry for short stays of up to 60 days without needing a paid eTA, leaving more room in your budget for safaris and coastal stays.

Rwanda

Not everyone wants their year-end holiday to feel like a non-stop sprint, and Rwanda is built for travellers who prefer scenery, clean air, and an unhurried pace. Days in Kigali easily revolve around specialty coffee shops, contemporary art at Inema Arts Center, and a sobering, essential visit to the Kigali Genocide Memorial before you head out into the countryside. From the capital, you can track chimpanzees and walk above the trees in Nyungwe Forest, go on wildlife drives in Akagera National Park, or spend quiet afternoons along the shores of Lake Kivu. With 30-day visa-free entry for Nigerian passport holders, getting there is straightforward from start to finish.

Mauritius

Sometimes a proper Christmas break calls for leaving mainland schedules behind altogether for turquoise lagoons, catamaran cruises, and mountain trails. In Mauritius, you can base yourself around Grand Baie in the north for boat trips to Île aux Cerfs and lively beachside dinners, or head south-west toward Le Morne Brabant for coastal hikes and water sports. Between beach days, the bustling Central Market in Port Louis, the lush trails of Black River Gorges National Park, and Casela Nature Parks keep a week-long itinerary full without ever feeling hectic. Nigerian travellers receive a free 14-day visa on arrival, though you will need to fill out Mauritius’s free All-in-One Travel Digital Form and Health Declaration Form online before boarding.

Ghana

Staying close to home does not mean settling for the same routine, especially when Accra turns into one of West Africa’s busiest festive hubs every December. You can spend mornings browsing contemporary art at Gallery 1957 and walking through historic Jamestown, afternoons unwinding at Labadi Beach or Kokrobite, and nights hopping between concerts and street-food spots. Whenever you are ready for a change of scenery, a road trip to Cape Coast and Elmina brings historic castles and the treetop canopy walkway at Kakum National Park within easy reach, while Aburi and Akosombo offer cooler hills and riverside views. Thanks to ECOWAS free movement, Nigerian passport holders enter Ghana visa-free for up to 90 days by air or road.

Côte d’Ivoire

For a West African holiday with a distinct francophone rhythm, Côte d’Ivoire pairs cosmopolitan city life with laid-back coastal escapes just a short flight from Nigeria. Abidjan greets visitors with lagoon views, leafy walking trails inside Banco National Park, and vibrant late-night dining in Zone 4 and Cocody where grilled fish and attiéké steal the show. A quick drive east takes you to Grand-Bassam for quiet beaches, craft markets, and historic architecture, while Assinie offers resort-style downtime further along the coast. Covered under ECOWAS visa-free access for up to 90 days, it is an easy switch-up when you want familiar regional warmth with a fresh cultural flavour.

item.title: From Tunde Kelani to Akinola Davies Jr., 5 Nollywood Directors You Should Know
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.category: King Of Boys: The Return of The King
item.description:
Tunde Kelani, Akinola Davies Jr., Kemi Adetiba, Daniel Etim Effiong, and Dammy Twitch represent five Nigerian film directors shaping Nollywood across classic adaptations, award-winning dramas, and box-office hits.

The post From Tunde Kelani to Akinola Davies Jr., 5 Nollywood Directors You Should Know appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
From music visuals to international festival stages and actor-turned-director debuts, Dammy Twitch, Akinola Davies Jr., and Daniel Etim Effiong represent different paths into Nollywood directing.

Think about the Nigerian films and series you have watched recently, the ones that kept you glued to your screen, had you talking about the storyline long after the credits rolled or recommending them to everyone you know. While the actors are often the faces you remember first, there is someone behind the camera whose creative choices help bring those stories to life: the director.

From interpreting the script and guiding actors to shaping how each scene looks, sounds and unfolds, directors influence almost every part of what ends up on screen. As Nollywood grows in ambition, production quality and global reach, the filmmakers steering these projects are becoming just as central to the industry’s story as the stars in front of the lens. Some have spent decades bringing Nigerian literature and history to the screen, while others are earning international acclaim or crossing over from music videos into feature films. Here are five Nollywood directors whose work is worth knowing.

Tunde Kelani

Start with Tunde Kelani if you want to see where modern Nigerian cinema found its literary and cultural roots. Trained at the London Film School after cutting his teeth in photography and television, the Mainframe Films founder has spent decades turning Nigerian literature, stage plays, and history into lasting screen works.

Titles like Ti Oluwa Nile, Koseegbe, O Le Ku, Saworoide, Thunderbolt: Magun, The Narrow Path, Maami, Dazzling Mirage, Ayinla, and Cordelia show how wide his range goes. Across years of festivals and awards, Kelani has collected major honours for his craft, and his adaptation Cordelia earned him a Best Director nomination at the 2026 Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards.

Tunde Kelani, whose directing catalogue spans Ti Oluwa Nile, Saworoide, The Narrow Path, Maami, and Cordelia, with Kunle Afolayan outdoors. Photo Credit: Tunde Kelani/Instagram

Akinola Davies Jr.

Few directors have linked global festival stages with homegrown Nollywood triumphs quite like Akinola Davies Jr. After his short film Lizard won the Short Film Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival in 2021, he co-wrote and directed his feature debut My Father’s Shadow alongside his brother Wale Davies.

The drama made history in 2025 as the first Nigerian film selected for the Official Selection at the Cannes Film Festival, picking up a Special Mention for the Caméra d’Or before winning Best Director at the British Independent Film Awards and Breakthrough Director at the Gotham Independent Film Awards. His momentum rolled straight into 2026 with a BAFTA win for Outstanding Debut by a British Writer, Director or Producer, followed by Best Director and Best Overall Movie wins at the 2026 AMVCAs.

Akinola Davies Jr. with his BAFTA trophy for My Father’s Shadow. Photo Credit: Akinola Davies Jr./Instagram

Kemi Adetiba

Before crossing into cinema and streaming, Kemi Adetiba built a reputation directing memorable music videos for artists including Wizkid, Tiwa Savage, Olamide, and Banky W.

On the big screen, she shattered box-office records with The Wedding Party and followed up with the crime drama King of Boys, its sequel King of Boys: The Return of the King, and the series To Kill a Monkey. Her sharp pacing, bold casting, and distinct visual style have kept her in the spotlight across platforms such as The Headies, the City People Entertainment Awards, and the AMVCAs.

Kemi Adetiba and Bucci Franklin on the set of To Kill a Monkey. Photo Credit: Kemi Adetiba/Instagram

Daniel Etim Effiong

Many movie lovers know Daniel Etim Effiong first as a familiar leading man across Nollywood films and streaming hits, yet his work behind the camera is just as central to his career.

Having studied filmmaking at AFDA in South Africa and gained experience on shorts and television episodes, he stepped into feature directing with the thriller The Herd. That debut brought him Best Director and Best Debut Feature Film by a Director nominations at the 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards, while The Herd collected three AMAA trophies and earned nine AMVCA nominations, including Best Director.

Daniel Etim Effiong on the set of The Herd which leads the 12th AMVCA nominations with 9 nods including Best Director.

Dammy Twitch

Known for years for directing visually bold music videos for stars like Davido, Burna Boy, and Omah Lay, Dammy Twitch (Apampa Oluwadamilola Owolabi) made his feature film directing debut in May 2026 with the romantic comedy Call of My Life.

Led by Uzoamaka Power and Andrew Yaw Bunting alongside Zubby Michael, Beverly Osu, Nkem Owoh, Patience Ozokwor, and Broda Shaggi, the film crossed ₦900 million at the Nigerian box office to become one of the highest-grossing Nollywood releases of 2026, while also winning the Favourite Feature Narrative Audience Award at the 2026 BlackStar Film Festival. Bringing his instincts for framing, colour, and pacing from music visuals into narrative cinema, he has quickly become a fresh voice movie fans are keeping a close eye on.

Dammy Twitch on the set of Call of My Life. Photo Credit: Dammy Twitch/Instagram

item.title: Esther Adeyanju: This International Men’s Day, Let’s Make Room for Men’s Vulnerability
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.description:
Written by Esther Adeyanju.

The post Esther Adeyanju: This International Men’s Day, Let’s Make Room for Men’s Vulnerability appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
“Men are not wired to show emotions.” A male friend once said to me during an argument. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured.

According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made.

“So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed.

He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature.

Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine?

The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.”

Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard.

Frequent questions men are asked: “How far? Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?”

We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears?

A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about.

We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean.

Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success.

A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful?

Surely, a man’s worth cannot be reduced to his bank balance, job title or ability to convince everyone that he has everything under control. There must be room for men who are still becoming. 

The Empty Chair Nobody Notices

This year’s theme for International Men’s Day, celebrated on November 19th, is “The Future Is Everyone.” While this theme may seem straightforward, it invites us to explore the true meaning of “everyone.”

Working in corporate communications at the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria (CIPM) has heightened my awareness of how easily we categorise people based on their roles: leaders, employees, fathers, mothers, young professionals, and others. However, behind every label is a human being whose story is often more complex than it appears.

The theme urges us to see people beyond face value, beyond titles and see them as humans first. It urges us to avoid assuming we know what others need. Allowing men to share their struggles does not diminish the experiences of another gender. Compassion is not a competition; there is ample space to challenge the expectations that confine both men and women.

After all, what kind of future can belong to everyone if some individuals must conceal parts of themselves to fit in?

This International Men’s Day, let’s celebrate the men who show up for their families, mentor young people, support their communities, and quietly make life better for others.

Let’s remember the weary men—those who haven’t achieved everything they envisioned, who fear disappointing their families, and who desperately need help but have been taught that asking for assistance makes them less of a man.

Reach out to your brother, check in on your father, and connect with that friend who always seems to have everything figured out.

I still disagree with my friend’s belief that men were not created to show emotions. Men are human beings, not machines programmed to absorb every disappointment without showing vulnerability. If the future truly belongs to everyone, it must also include men who are allowed to be vulnerable, uncertain, imperfect, and human.

We have spent generations teaching men to stand strong, but it’s time we remind them that they don’t always have to stand alone.

item.title: Burna Boy, Asake & Seyi Vibez Bring Afrobeats to the World of GTA VI
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Burna Boy, Asake, and Seyi Vibez feature in Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI, which launches on 19 November 2026 with Burna Boy co-hosting AfroBank FM alongside songs including "Joha," "Giza," and "Bigger."

The post Burna Boy, Asake & Seyi Vibez Bring Afrobeats to the World of GTA VI appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
From left: Nigerian artists Asake, Seyi Vibez, and Burna Boy, whose songs appear in Grand Theft Auto VI.

How else could Grand Theft Auto VI begin than with Nigerian artists featured in the music lineup of the biggest video game release of the year? As players around the world finally step into Rockstar Games’ highly anticipated open-world action-adventure title, Burna Boy, Asake, and Seyi Vibez are making sure Nigerian music is front and centre on the virtual streets of Vice City and the wider state of Leonida.

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) officially arrives today, Thursday, 19 November 2026, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, ending a 13-year wait since Grand Theft Auto V first hit consoles. Developed and published by Rockstar Games, the open-world action-adventure game follows dual protagonists Jason and Lucia across the sun-soaked, neon-lit state of Leonida—a fictional take on Florida that brings players back to Vice City in the franchise’s largest map yet. Music has always been at the heart of the Grand Theft Auto universe, where players tune into curated in-game radio stations while driving or walking around town, and this sixth instalment takes African soundscapes seriously.

At the centre of the Nigerian presence is AfroBank FM, a dedicated African music radio station inside Grand Theft Auto VI that is co-hosted by Grammy winner Burna Boy—credited on-air simply as Burna—alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax, who goes by Palmsy. Curated to spotlight everything from 20th-century African classics to contemporary Afrobeats, amapiano, and 3-step, the station features Asake’s 2022 hit “Joha” from his debut album Mr Money With The Vibe, as well as “Giza“, the 2023 collaboration between Burna Boy and Seyi Vibez from Burna Boy’s seventh studio album I Told Them…. Alongside those tracks, Burna Boy also appears on the game’s official companion soundtrack album, Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, with his original song “Bigger” sitting on a 34-track roster that includes Travis Scott, Cardi B, Dua Lipa, SZA, Tame Impala, and Lana Del Rey.

The African representation on AfroBank FM stretches beyond Nigeria too, sharing airwaves with Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor on “Gye Wani” and South African stars DJ Lag, Robot Boii, and Kamo Mphela on “Shay’sana“. With players able to listen to Leonida’s terrestrial radio stations both in vehicles and on foot through in-game headphones, millions of gamers worldwide are now cruising through Vice City with Burna Boy on the mic and Asake and Seyi Vibez on heavy rotation.

item.title: How La Roche-Posay Brought Skin Science to Over 500 Guests in Its First Living Lab Experience
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
The three-day experience brought together consumers, healthcare professionals and skincare experts for interactive demonstrations, expert-led discussions and conversations around skin health.

The post How La Roche-Posay Brought Skin Science to Over 500 Guests in Its First Living Lab Experience appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
La Roche-Posay concluded its first Living Lab experience in Nigeria, welcoming Nigerian stakeholders to its opening party and three-day programme, held from 4 to 6 November 2026 at Oasis by The Five Palm, Victoria Island, Lagos.

Inspired by the original Living Lab concept in Paris, the experience brought the science, research and expertise behind skincare closer to Nigerian consumers and healthcare professionals. It marked the brand’s first Living Lab in the country, creating a platform for more accessible conversations around skin health, dermatological innovation and everyday skincare.

The experience opened with an exclusive session for healthcare professionals and invited guests before welcoming members of the public over the following two days. Each day featured three expert-led sessions exploring the role of dermatology and scientific research in advancing skin health, the wider impact of skin conditions on everyday life, and the importance of understanding product safety, tolerance and efficacy. The sessions brought together healthcare professionals and representatives from across Nigeria’s dermatological beauty and skincare community, encouraging knowledge-sharing and stronger connections between science, expertise and consumer education.

Visitors explored five dedicated Innovation Corners showcasing La Roche-Posay’s Effaclar, Mela B3, Anthelios, Cicaplast and Lipikar ranges. Each space introduced visitors to specific skin concerns and the science behind the brand’s product formulations.

Through interactive demonstrations and guided product experiences, guests gained a better understanding of different skin concerns and the role of targeted skincare in addressing them. At the Anthelios corner, visitors used a UV camera to see the effects of ultraviolet exposure and better understand the importance of sun protection. The Effaclar and Mela B3 spaces explored concerns including blemishes and hyperpigmentation, while the Cicaplast and Lipikar corners introduced visitors to approaches to caring for sensitive, damaged and dry skin.

Beyond the Innovation Corners, visitors explored the Blue House, which presented La Roche-Posay’s history and commitment to dermatological innovation, and the Scars of Life Cinema. The cinema screened a 25-minute film exploring the physical and psychological realities of living with scars and scarring, including their impact on self-image and everyday life. The film also highlighted how Lipikar supports the care of skin affected by scarring, bringing attention to the importance of addressing both the visible and less visible experiences associated with skin conditions.

The programme also created opportunities for visitors to engage with skincare experts and dermatologists through one-on-one consultations, ask questions about their individual skin concerns and receive guidance on building appropriate skincare routines. Visitors could then explore and purchase recommended products at the Konga pop-up, with discounts of up to 15% available.

“Skin conditions should not be treated based on assumptions or advice picked up from social media. Acne, hyperpigmentation, eczema and other concerns can have different underlying causes and require different approaches to management. Using the wrong products or adopting unsuitable routines can aggravate existing concerns rather than improve them,” said Dr Folakemi Cole-Adeife, Consultant Physician and Dermatologist, and member of the L’Oréal Dermatologist Beauty MedSquad. “This is why initiatives like La Roche-Posay’s Living Lab are valuable. They create opportunities to bridge the gap between dermatological knowledge and everyday skincare decisions, helping people understand their skin and make more informed choices based on their actual needs, rather than trends or trial and error.”

Reflecting on the experience, Anaïs Routhiau, Business Development Manager, LID, L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty, Sub-Saharan Africa, said:

“The Living Lab provided an opportunity to bring La Roche-Posay’s heritage, dermatological expertise and commitment to skin health closer to Nigerian consumers. Across the programme, we engaged with healthcare professionals and members of the public, creating opportunities for people to learn more about their skin and understand how dermatological science informs the products we develop. It was encouraging to see the interest in skin health education and the level of engagement throughout the experience.”

The first edition of the Living Lab Nigeria marked an important opportunity for La Roche-Posay to strengthen its engagement with consumers and the medical community, bringing dermatological knowledge, product education and practical conversations about skin health into one shared experience.

item.content:encoded:
A historic hosting line-up spanning five African countries and a first-of-its-kind AI assistant named Infinity set the stage for a distinctive celebration as The Future Awards Africa (TFAA) marked its 20th edition on Saturday, 14 November 2026. Held at the Balmoral Convention Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos, the ceremony brought together young achievers, industry leaders and public figures to celebrate two decades of recognizing African excellence.

Themed “Celebrating the Redefiners: Africa’s AI Generation,” the evening honoured young Africans aged 18 to 35 across 26 categories, including technology and innovation, entrepreneurship, governance, music, film, literature, advocacy, sports and fashion. Their achievements formed the heart of a milestone edition that celebrated the platform’s legacy while embracing new possibilities for its stage.

The event was hosted by Nigerian actress and trained lawyer Genoveva Umeh; Claudia Naisabwa, a Kenyan media personality and host; Priscilla Kayira, a Malawian radio broadcaster and television personality; Resego Motlhokathari, a television and radio host from Botswana; and Idris Sultan, a Tanzanian actor and former Big Brother Africa winner.

Together, the five hosts gave the anniversary celebration a distinctly continental presence. Bringing different voices, personalities and perspectives to the proceedings, the line-up reflected the reach of an awards platform whose story has grown alongside the generations of young Africans it recognises.

The hosts also shared the spotlight with Infinity, an AI assistant that introduced another dimension to the evening. With a distinct voice, quick wit, and playful responses, Infinity engaged with the hosts, drawing laughter and creating unexpected, exciting moments throughout the ceremony. Its appearance offered an exciting glimpse into how artificial intelligence is influencing not only the way people work and create, but also how audiences experience entertainment.

Sharp Band and the Loud Urban Choir also entertained guests with captivating musical performances, adding to the evening’s celebratory atmosphere.

At the heart of the celebration were the winners and the work that earned them recognition. Nora Awolowo received the Prize for Young Person of the Year, Teniola Aladese won the Prize for Acting, and Olamidun Ogundoyin took home the Prize for Entrepreneurship. Pastor Jerry Uchechukwu Eze, who was represented at the ceremony by media personality Hero Daniels, received the Prize for Service to Young People.

The ceremony welcomed representatives of distinguished public figures, including Hon. Mobolaji Abubakre Ogunlende, Lagos State Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, who represented the Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu. The first winners of The Future Awards Africa Independent (TFAAi), a state-level initiative established in 2026 to discover young changemakers whose contributions may receive limited visibility on national platforms, were also recognised. Beginning with Rivers, Abia, Oyo and Kano States, TFAAi brings the awards’ vision closer to the communities where these young people live and work. Their introduction at the milestone edition connected local achievement with the wider continental celebration.

Reflecting on the significance of the milestone edition, Ayodeji Razaq, Executive Director of The Future Awards Africa, said,

“Twenty editions represent a sustained belief in the young Africans who continue to shape the continent’s future, and a responsibility to recognise their achievements with the seriousness they deserve. Across generations, our honourees have shown what becomes possible when talent is matched with conviction, discipline and a commitment to others. This year’s Redefiners carry that legacy into a period of profound change, bringing original ideas and sound judgement to the opportunities before them. As we expand recognition into more communities through TFAAi, our ambition is to ensure that exceptional work can be seen wherever it happens. Twenty years in, we remain committed to celebrating remarkable young Africans”.

TFAA co-founders Chude Jideonwo and Adebola Williams also reflected on the journey from the platform’s beginnings to its 20th edition. They highlighted the generations of young achievers whose stories have shaped the awards and the importance of continuing to create space for emerging talent.

Supported by OPay, Amstel Malta, Optiva Capital, Knorr, Brila Media, Ebewele Brown, Lagos State Ministry of Tourism, Art, and Culture and other sponsors and media partners, the milestone edition brought that history into conversation with the future. Its five-country hosting line-up reflected the continental breadth of the celebration, while Infinity’s presence introduced a fresh approach and set the tone for the future of awards ceremonies across the continent. The presence of the inaugural TFAAi winners added another significant dimension, connecting achievements within local communities to a wider African stage.

item.content:encoded:
One of the best aspects of art is its ability to imitate current events or imagine possibilities. Movies, as a powerful art form, present a sequence of events that allows viewers to see reflections of themselves or envision who they could become.

At its core, art exists to entertain, inform and critique society. Through films, music and visual expressions, we are continually reminded of our shared humanity—our joys, flaws and contradictions.

One subject that art, particularly film, has explored is masculinity. However, this theme is often addressed subtly and can be easy to overlook, as the movies that dominate global box offices frequently focus on spectacle: fantasy, romance, adventure or others. Conversations about men, their inner lives, vulnerabilities and social roles are often not in the top circle.

Nonetheless, some films have attempted to explore what it means to be a man in today’s world. They invite audiences to contemplate important questions such as: What is the role of men in society? What defines a man? How does a man’s behaviour influence those around him? What expectations does society place on men? What responsibilities do men have within society? Where does responsibility begin, and where does it end? Do men matter? Do their feelings matter?

The theme for this year’s International Men’s Day is “The Future Is For Everyone.” For that, here are some movies that explore and illuminate the complexities of masculinity:

The Pursuit of Happyness

This classic film reveals the vulnerability often hidden behind male perseverance. Will Smith’s portrayal of Chris Gardner challenges the stoic notion of manhood by showing fatherhood as both an act of love and endurance. Through his struggles with homelessness, rejection, and exhaustion, the film redefines masculinity, depicting it as the courage to remain tender even when life tests your strength in every way.

Fatherhood

Kevin Hart’s film Fatherhood delves into themes of grief and single parenthood, balancing humour with heartfelt moments. It challenges traditional expectations of masculinity by illustrating a father’s journey through uncertainty, learning empathy, and committing to being present for his child/ren. Through this film, Kevin Hart shares his vision of what it means to be a man and a father.

Adolescence

Adolescence examines how boys internalise distorted notions of strength and freedom, and how escaping them demands emotional awareness. The film reveals the journey of a young boy on the brink of adulthood, revealing the pressures of identity and self-definition. There is a lot to unpack from Stephen Graham’s Adolescence about what it means to be a father and a child.

King Richard

A faction. In the narrative, King Richard shares the stories of Serena and Venus Williams, highlighting discipline and belief as fundamental expressions of a father’s love. Richard Williams’ journey illustrates his complex relationship with ambition, protection, and vulnerability. His flaws and passion are deeply intertwined. The film reveals that masculinity can be both an act of dominance and devotion, which can be a powerful drive to nurture greatness, even when the world fails to recognise it.

Breath of Life

Directed by BB Sasore, masculinity is explored in Breath of Life through faith, purpose and regret. It tells of a man who retreats from the world after loss. Although he finds renewal through mentoring a young man, the film portrays redemption and emotional reconnection as masculine virtues.

My Father’s Shadow

Akinola Davies Jr‘s My Father’s Shadow examines how sons absorb both the strengths and the wounds of their fathers, and how healing demands confrontation. By unpacking silence, trauma, and reconciliation, it shows that breaking cycles is an act of love, not rebellion.

item.content:encoded:
Growing up, Tunji Olowolafe’s parents brought the family to Are-Ekiti every Christmas, and a trip to Ikogosi was compulsory. Decades later, he returned to the warm springs town with family, friends and business partners, “not to take away, but to help build something enduring in Ekiti.”

Speaking as Chairman and Chief Launcher of Ikogosi Day 2026, Thanksgiving and Launch of the Oba’s Palace Project, on Saturday, 14 November 2026, the Chancellor of Ekiti State University set out a vision for Ikogosi built on intentional tourism, enterprise and heritage.

Dr. Olowolafe said Ikogosi’s task now is to give visitors compelling reasons to come, stay longer and spend across local businesses. He pointed to the recent Ikogosi 17.5km Race, which drew runners from across Nigeria alongside athletes from Ghana, Kenya and Ethiopia, as an example of what happens when private initiative meets local hospitality. He urged the same thinking for lifestyle and executive tourism, with the ambition of making Ikogosi a premier international destination for weddings, milestone birthdays, corporate retreats and landmark gatherings.

“Our natural landscape will draw people in. But only the quality of the experience we deliver, through warmth of welcome, impeccable service and attention to detail, will bring them back,” he said.

To build that service culture, he called for a deeper, structured partnership between the Ikogosi Resort and the Hospitality Management Technology Department of the Federal Polytechnic, Ado-Ekiti, which has already produced two sets of National Diploma graduates. The goal is for students to train alongside seasoned professionals while serving real guests. He also proposed alliances with leading international hospitality institutes to benchmark local teaching and service, noting that world-class hospitality must become Ekiti’s signature.

He argued that the same commercial discipline must apply to the resources beneath the ground.

“It is not enough to say we have clay or kaolin. We must ask: What are their exact industrial specifications? What can we competitively manufacture? And who is ready to buy?” he said.

He tasked the Department of Geology at Ekiti State University, headed by Professor Yinka Aturamu, with establishing precise data on local deposits and mapping out what it would take to turn them into viable commercial enterprises. For him, the measure of success is what it changes for young people in the community.

“For a young person growing up in Ikogosi, the result must be tangible: a marketable skill, a steady job, a supply contract or a thriving enterprise,” he said.

He cited Rasheed Sarumi’s Saroafrica Group as proof of what is possible. The group acquired Gossy Warm Springs in 2018 and restored the plant to full production in 2019. Together with its partners, Saroafrica is now investing US$25 million in a manufacturing facility in Ikogosi, which will run on its own 2MW gas-fired power plant.

On the Oba’s Palace Project, Dr. Olowolafe said its primary purpose is to uphold the traditional institution and unite the community. He urged that it also be designed to preserve and showcase Ikogosi’s heritage, “so that visitors meet not merely a scenic resort, but a proud people with a rich story to tell.”

As Chief Launcher, he formally launched the project and invited sons and daughters of Ikogosi, business leaders and friends of the community to help surpass the ₦1 billion target. Ahead of the launch, more than thirty-five individuals in Lagos and Abuja had already stepped forward to support the cause.

Reflecting on his childhood visits, Dr. Olowolafe closed with a personal note.

“I enjoyed Ikogosi as a young boy. It will give me infinitely greater joy to see today’s children grow up knowing they can build a prosperous future right here at home,” he said.

item.content:encoded:
From left: Miss Universe Democratic Republic of the Congo 2026 Jessi Kalambayi, Miss Universe Namibia 2026 Charene Labuschagne, and Miss Universe Botswana 2026 Dabilo Moses ahead of the 75th Miss Universe finale in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The Miss Universe stage is getting a beautiful dose of African representation this year, with 17 contestants from across the continent making their way to Puerto Rico for the pageant’s 75th edition. And there are plenty of stories to discover among them, from Uganda’s historic debut to Nigeria’s Danielle Adewusi, whose journey to the competition comes with a lovely family connection.

Taking place in San Juan, Puerto Rico, the Diamond Anniversary edition will bring together 116 contestants from around the world, all hoping to claim the newly unveiled 75th-anniversary crown, The Radiance of an Eternal Legacy. The grand finale is scheduled for Tuesday, 24 November 2026, at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum.

This year’s show will be hosted by R’Bonney Gabriel, Mario Lopez, Zuri Hall and Dayanara Torres. At the end of the night, reigning Miss Universe 2025 Fátima Bosch of Mexico will pass on her crown to a new winner. Bosch took the title in Thailand last November, ahead of contestants from Thailand, Venezuela, the Philippines and Côte d’Ivoire.

For Africa, the road to this year’s competition has come with a few changes. Angola, the Republic of the Congo, South Sudan, Zambia and Zimbabwe were unable to participate due to U.S. travel and visa restrictions, while Côte d’Ivoire, Mauritius, Rwanda and Senegal withdrew from the competition. Still, 17 African countries have contestants in the running, including Uganda, which is making its historic Miss Universe debut. Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Tunisia are among the countries returning to the global stage.

Representing Nigeria is 29-year-old medical doctor and women’s health advocate Danielle Adewusi, also known as Danielle Fadeke Adewusi. Her participation adds a special family detail to the story: she won Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 in Lagos, 35 years after her mother, Tonia Okogbenin, represented the country at Miss Universe 1991.

From first-time participation to familiar faces returning to the competition, these are the 17 African beauty queens representing the continent at Miss Universe 2026.

Dabilo Moses — Botswana

Representing Botswana is 26-year-old Dabilo Moses from Gaborone (born in Tutume). A Broadcasting and Journalism student at Limkokwing University of Creative Technology, she previously won Miss Independence Botswana 2022, reached the Top 24 at Miss Supranational 2023 as Botswana’s first-ever entrant, and was appointed Miss Universe Botswana 2026 after finishing as first runner-up in 2025.

Miss Universe Botswana 2026 Dabilo Moses at the 75th Miss Universe competition in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Audrey Black — Cameroon

After Cameroon’s brief absence from the pageant, 30-year-old Audrey Black (Audrey Black Moutongo) from Douala is carrying the nation’s flag in San Juan. Crowned Miss Cameroon, the Paris-educated entrepreneur is bringing Cameroonian culture and determination back to the Miss Universe stage.

Miss Universe Cameroon 2026 Audrey Black ahead of the 75th Miss Universe competition in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Armandina Cunha — Cape Verde

Following Cape Verde’s debut at the pageant in 2025, 27-year-old Armandina Cunha from Mindelo steps onto the international stage as the country’s second-ever Miss Universe representative.

Miss Universe Cape Verde 2026 Armandina Cunha at the 75th Miss Universe competition in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Jessi Kalambayi — Democratic Republic of the Congo

Representing the Democratic Republic of the Congo is 28-year-old Jessi Kalambayi from Kinshasa. No stranger to high-stakes pageantry, she previously held the title of Miss Colorado USA 2024 and placed in the Top 10 at Miss USA 2024 before winning the Miss Universe DRC 2026 crown in Kinshasa.

Miss Universe Democratic Republic of the Congo 2026 Jessi Kalambayi at the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Sonia Gergis — Egypt

Flying the flag for Egypt is 32-year-old Sonia Gergis from Cairo, bringing North African representation and seasoned poise to the 116-woman lineup in Puerto Rico.

Miss Universe Egypt 2026 Sonia Gergis at the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Isabel Mbomio — Equatorial Guinea

At 24 years old, Isabel Mbomio from Evinayong is representing Equatorial Guinea at the 75th Miss Universe competition, continuing the Central African nation’s presence on the global stage.

Miss Universe Equatorial Guinea 2026 Isabel Mbomio ahead of the 75th Miss Universe competition in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Bruk Belete — Ethiopia

Ethiopia makes its return to Miss Universe with 24-year-old Bruk Belete (Bruktawit Belete Woldeyes) of Addis Ababa, marking the East African country’s comeback to the international pageant.

Miss Universe Ethiopia 2026 Bruk Belete ahead of the 75th Miss Universe finale in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Belvy Ofori — Ghana

Representing Ghana is 33-year-old Belvy Ofori from Accra. Having spent the lead-up to Puerto Rico sharing her journey and preparation across Ghanaian media, she is aiming to build on West Africa’s strong recent run at the competition.

Miss Universe Ghana 2026 Belvy Ofori ahead of the 75th Miss Universe finale in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Justine Kamara — Guinea

Also flying the flag for West Africa is 29-year-old Justine Kamara, who represents Guinea in San Juan alongside the 115 other international delegates.

Miss Universe Guinea 2026 Justine Kamara ahead of the 75th Miss Universe finale in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Jean Ojiro — Kenya

Kenya returns to the Miss Universe fold with 27-year-old Jean Ojiro from Nyanza, bringing East African elegance back to the competition after the country sat out the previous edition.

Miss Universe Kenya 2026 Jean Ojiro ahead of the 75th Miss Universe finale in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Charene Labuschagne — Namibia

Representing Namibia is 28-year-old Charene Labuschagne from Windhoek, continuing the Southern African nation’s consistent run at the global pageant.

Miss Universe Namibia 2026 Charene Labuschagne at the 75th Miss Universe competition in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Danielle Adewusi — Nigeria

Nigeria’s representative, 29-year-old Danielle Adewusi (Danielle Fadeke Adewusi) from Lagos, brings together a background in medicine, pageantry, and advocacy. A King’s College London graduate with an MBBS in Medicine and a first-class BSc in Psychology, she previously placed Top 5 at Miss Universe Great Britain 2023 before winning Miss Universe Nigeria 2026. In San Juan, she is championing her women’s health initiative, “Scrub the Stigma,” while following in the footsteps of her mother, Tonia Okogbenin, who competed at Miss Universe in 1991.

Dr Danielle Adewusi crowned as Miss Universe Nigeria 2026.

Katti Fofanah — Sierra Leone

Sierra Leone makes a welcome return to Miss Universe with 22-year-old Katti Fofanah, one of the youngest African contestants in this year’s competition.

Miss Universe Sierra Leone 2026 Katti Fofanah representing Sierra Leone at the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Bajabulise Thela — South Africa

Representing South Africa is 23-year-old Bajabulise Thela from Mpumalanga, carrying the legacy of one of the pageant’s most decorated African nations into the 75th-anniversary finale.

Miss Universe South Africa 2026 Bajabulise Thela at the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Representing Tanzania is 30-year-old Elizabeth Makune from Mwanza, flying the Tanzanian flag in Puerto Rico as part of East Africa’s contingent.

Miss Universe Tanzania 2026 Elizabeth Makune representing Tanzania at the 75th Miss Universe competition in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The Woof Studios Africa event, held in partnership with Insight Redefini, put original intellectual property, creator-led storytelling and long-term brand partnerships at the centre of the conversation.

item.content:encoded:
The evolving business of content creation took centre stage in Lagos as Woof Studios Africa, in partnership with Insight Redefini, hosted the second edition of PluggedIN 2026 in Victoria Island, Lagos.

The gathering brought together some of Nigeria’s leading content creators, filmmakers, advertising professionals and brand executives to explore how digital influence can translate into original intellectual property, sustainable creative businesses and longer-term commercial opportunities.

Hosted by actress and media personality Bisola Aiyeola, the event gave creators a platform to present original concepts and explore new possibilities for collaboration with brands and industry stakeholders.

From Content Creation to Intellectual Property

A major highlight of PluggedIN 2026 was its creator showcase, featuring Taaooma, Layi Wasabi, Aproko Doctor, Ify’s Kitchen, Biodun Stephen, Osas Ighodaro, Shank Comics, Folagade Banks, Afropolitan, Bolaji Ogunmola, and Geena Foodies n Spice.

The creators presented original ideas, show formats and potential collaborative projects, offering a glimpse into the range of stories and formats emerging from Nigeria’s creative community.

The opportunity for brands lies in being part of that process through partnerships that go beyond individual sponsored posts to support the development, production and distribution of original content.

For Adetutu Laditan, Creator Economy Catalyst and Founder of Woof Studios Africa, this shift requires a more structured approach to supporting creators and connecting them with the right opportunities.

“Our vision at Woof Studios Africa has always been to empower African creators to move beyond virality and build lasting, profitable enterprises. Nigerian creators are thinking bigger, and forward-thinking brands want to be part of that evolution,” she said.

Laditan explained that Woof Studios works across the business and production aspects of content development, including funding and distribution, to help creators take ideas beyond their initial digital formats.

“When creators understand a brand’s business objectives, and brands respect the authentic voice a creator has spent years cultivating, we stop simply buying attention and start co-creating stories that matter.”

The conversations at PluggedIN also addressed the realities of building sustainable creative businesses.

During the creator-focused panel, Kiekie, Craze Clown, Jay On-Air and Winifred Nwania of Zeelicious Food discussed the opportunities and challenges of building careers in the digital space. They explored content ownership, audience engagement, monetisation and the importance of meaningful brand relationships.

The discussions reflected an increasingly important question for the industry: How can creators turn the audiences and cultural influence they have built into sustainable businesses?

The opportunity is significant, but so are the challenges. The Africa Creator Economy Report 2026 estimates the continent’s creator economy at about $3 billion, with the potential to reach $17.8 billion by 2030. The report also highlights the monetisation gap facing creators, with about six in ten surveyed earning less than $100 monthly from their creative work.

For Babatunde Olaifa, Group Chief Executive Officer at Insight Redefini, addressing this gap requires closer collaboration between brands and creators.

“This is not about an influencer campaign; this is about the creative economy space. We have to bring both parties together to tell stories that matter to the brand, to the creators, and to the audiences,” Olaifa stated.

“Brands can bring the investment and distribution needed to take an interesting format and turn it into a sustainable property. Our ambition as Insight Redefini is to bring our brands together with the biggest creators in Nigeria to create magic, and beyond that, to build and co-own IPs.”

The brand-focused panel further explored what this kind of collaboration could look like in practice. Participants included Adeyinka Jemi-Alade of TGI Group, Bolaji Popoola of Mondelez International, Chisom Bikawei of Nestlé Nigeria, Esosa Osagiede of Insight Redefini, Francis Obiajulu of Amstel Malta and Hi-Malt, and Sam Okolie of Guinness Nigeria.

Their discussion examined how brands can work more effectively with creators through integrated storytelling, stronger creative relationships and partnerships that deliver value beyond short-term campaign visibility.

A New Conversation for the Creator Economy

PluggedIN 2026 brought an important industry conversation into focus: the relationship between creators, brands and the business of content is changing.

As creators develop original formats and explore ownership of their intellectual property, brands can participate in creating stories that connect with audiences in more meaningful ways. Making that possible will require investment, production expertise, distribution and a clearer understanding of the value each party brings.

The next phase of the creator economy will not be defined by influence alone, but also by the ideas, businesses and intellectual property creators can build around it.

item.content:encoded:
What does it really mean to play to win in business and leadership? Beyond earning a seat at the table, it requires more than competence or professional accomplishments. It requires the confidence to own one’s value, the clarity to communicate one’s contributions and the intentionality to build visibility that translates into meaningful influence.

These conversations defined The Executive Woman Summit (TEWS) 2.0, which brought together hundreds of executive women, corporate professionals, entrepreneurs and emerging leaders at Harbour Point, Victoria Island, Lagos, on Wednesday, October 28, 2026.

Convened by Bola Matel-Okoh, a dual-qualified attorney (called to both the New York and Nigerian Bars), Executive Coach, Non-Executive Director at Wema Bank, and CEO of BMO Advisory Services, the second edition of the summit was themed Playing to Win: Elevate Your Vision, Value and Visibility. It provided an intentional platform for candid conversations, practical insights and strategic alliances on what it takes for women to advance, lead and thrive in today’s evolving corporate landscape.

In her opening address, Matel-Okoh challenged women to rethink how they approach professional visibility, authority and advancement. According to her, competence is merely the baseline; it is not enough if you are unwilling to communicate your value, own your voice and position yourself for higher-stakes opportunities.

This philosophy also came through in her cover interview with THISDAY Glitterati ahead of the summit, where she offered a compelling perspective on the distinction between holding a powerful position and exercising genuine influence.

“A powerful position gives you formal authority. Influence determines how deeply your leadership shapes people’s thinking, decisions and actions. A title may secure your place in a meeting, but credibility makes people listen,” she explained.

She also challenged the assumption that excellent work will automatically speak for itself, encouraging women to communicate their contributions with evidence and confidence.

“What problem did you solve? What result did you produce? What changed because of your leadership?” she asked, highlighting the importance of making professional value visible to the decision-makers who influence career progression and boardroom opportunities. “There is no need to diminish your achievements to make others comfortable. You can be gracious and still be clear about the value you bring,” she added.

The summit featured a distinguished line-up of women shaping leadership, business, finance, entertainment and corporate governance. Chairman of Ecobank Nigeria, Bola Adesola, and CEO of FS Global Advisory Services, Folake Sanu, delivered keynote addresses, sharing perspectives on leadership, professional growth, boardroom dynamics and navigating the demands of executive life.

One standout moment was the fireside conversation, The Architecture of Significance: Redefining What It Means to Win, featuring Founder of The Chair Centre Group, Ibukun Awosika, and Chairman of MTN Foundation, Dr Mosun Belo-Olusoga. Moderated by Bola Matel-Okoh, the conversation explored success beyond traditional measures, the importance of building lasting influence and the choices that shape a woman’s professional and personal legacy.

Two engaging panel discussions further unpacked the practical dimensions of visibility, influence and career advancement.

The first panel explored how women can build strategic relationships and turn professional networks into meaningful opportunities. Executive Coach and Relationship Counsellor Taiye Aluko moderated the discussion, which featured three members of Matel-Okoh’s corporate community for women, The Club House @ Caroline’s Place: Managing Director of Z-Edge Limited, Kikelomo Atanda-Owo; Chief Operating Officer at SAS Textiles, Toyin Bakare; and Izehi Anuge, Values and Character Strategist. Together, they addressed how trust, authentic connections and intentional relationship-building can help women navigate their careers and create growth opportunities.

The second panel focused on how women can raise their visibility, communicate their expertise and position themselves for greater opportunities. Moderated by Strategic Visibility Advisor Glory Edozien, the session featured Founder of Smart Stewards Financial Advisory, Sola Adesakin; Actor and Founder of Jalent Africa, Juliet Ibrahim; Media Personality and Talent Manager, Layole Oyatogun; and Head of Brands and Marketing Communications at Wema Bank, Mabel Adeteye.

Beyond the plenary conversations, TEWS 2.0 offered guests an elevated experience that blended leadership, lifestyle and high-level networking. Attendees arrived in polished, fashion-forward looks, bringing an unmistakable sense of style to the room. The programme also featured a live musical performance, an energising aerobic dance-along session, curated networking opportunities and brand exhibition booths, creating room for connection and interaction beyond the main stage.

More than a gathering of accomplished women, The Executive Woman Summit 2.0 reinforced the imperative of creating environments where women can access the relationships, knowledge and institutional support needed to advance. From recognising the contributions of established pioneers to equipping the next generation to step forward, TEWS 2.0 made a decisive case for a more intentional approach to women’s leadership in Africa.

To learn more about The Executive Woman Summit, visit https://bolamatelokoh.com/tews/. Stay connected with Bola Matel-Okoh, fondly known as Coach BMO, on LinkedIn and Instagram at @bolamatelokoh.

item.content:encoded:
The Metropolitan Club, Lagos, was transformed into a gathering of some of the most influential names in Nigeria’s energy industry as the Women in Energy Network (WIEN) hosted its 2026 Gala & Awards. Bringing together industry leaders, policymakers, corporate executives and other distinguished guests, the evening marked six years of WIEN’s advocacy for greater representation, inclusion and leadership opportunities for women across the energy value chain.

Beyond the glamour, elegant conversations and celebrations, the event carried a clear message: it is time to move beyond conversations about inclusion and focus on measurable progress.

The Honourable Minister of Women Affairs and Social Development, Hajia Imaan Sulaiman-Ibrahim, delivered the special address, ably represented by Dr Adedayo Benjamins-Laniyi, Director-General/Chief Executive Officer of the Maryam Babangida National Centre for Women Development.

In her address, WIEN President Eyono Fatayi-Williams emphasised that progress must be visible, measurable and sustained.

“As we celebrate six years, we also have to ask ourselves an important question: What do the next six years look like? Because we cannot spend the next six years having the same conversations we have had in the last six years. We cannot continue to talk about inclusion without asking what has changed,” Fatayi-Williams challenged the industry.

The evening also featured a keynote address by Dr Mutiu Sunmonu (CON), Chairman of The Sage Centre for Leadership Excellence, who shared perspectives on leadership and the importance of creating opportunities for women to contribute meaningfully to the sector.

Six Years of Building Opportunities for Women

Reflecting on the organisation’s growth and the realities of navigating the energy sector, WIEN Board of Trustees Chairperson, Dr Cecilia Aqua Umoren, challenged guests to strive for true parity.

“In the six years that WIEN has been in existence, we have created more opportunities for women, resulting in numerous appointments and an expanded STEM pipeline. However, progress is not parity; we are ultimately aiming for true parity. We must acknowledge that most leadership positions today are occupied by men, meaning we cannot achieve our objectives without partnering with them to create access. If the room is not created for you, create your own room, set your own table, and be at your own table.”

WIEN’s Executive Secretary, Asanimo Omezi, echoed this commitment, highlighting the network’s growth from a collective of 30 women to more than 1,000 members, supported by 30 corporate partners.

“We started as a small collective of just 30 women, and today we have grown to over a thousand members with thirty corporate partners. The newly unveiled DEI benchmark will move us from mere conversation to visible accountability. Ultimately, the plural of women you see here today sends a clear message: we are knowledgeable, we are competent, and we are ready to take what belongs to us,” Omezi said.

A New DEI Benchmark in Partnership with KPMG

One of the evening’s defining moments was the unveiling of the WIEN Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) Benchmark Report, developed in collaboration with KPMG.

Following remarks by Bimpe Afolabi, Partner at KPMG, the report was introduced as a tool for measuring diversity, equity and inclusion practices across the energy industry. Designed to move the conversation beyond intentions, the benchmark provides a framework for assessing workplace practices, representation and progress, helping organisations identify gaps and track improvements over time.

The launch marked an important step in WIEN’s commitment to making inclusion more measurable and accountable.

The programme also featured an executive leadership fireside chat, moderated by Rosario Osobase. The panel explored the critical role of male allyship and featured the Executive Director in charge of Human Resources at ExxonMobil Affiliates in Nigeria, Emem Abraham; Managing Director of Oando Energy Resources, Alex Irune; Managing Director/CEO of Seplat Energy, Effiong Okon; and Adeleye Falade, Managing Director of NLNG.

Among the insights shared was NLNG’s recent recruitment experience, where women accounted for more than half of applicants and 50% of selected candidates. This offered a practical example of how deliberate recruitment approaches can help broaden participation.

Celebrating the Women Making a Difference

A major highlight of the gala was the presentation of the Winning With Women Awards (WIWA), recognising women and organisations making notable contributions to Nigeria’s energy industry.

Among the individual honourees, Folake Soetan received the WIEN Woman of the Year and Outstanding Woman in Power awards. Moroti Adeyinka Adedoyin received the Lifetime Achievement Award, while Bassey Adie was recognised as Female Energy Entrepreneur of the Year and Outstanding Woman in Midstream, Gas and Energy Logistics.

Other award recipients included Caroline Eboumbou for her contribution to renewable energy; Funmi Ogbue for her advocacy for girls in STEM and energy; Maryamu Idris for leadership in the downstream sector; and Judith Ikwuwunna, named Emerging Woman in Energy (Rising Star).

Corporate and institutional recognition went to ExxonMobil and Seplat Energy Plc, jointly named Corporate Champion for Women-Owned Energy Businesses; Seplat Energy Plc, recognised for Excellence in Diverse Leadership; the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), named Public Sector Champion for Women in Energy; and Telmek Global Resources, named Employer of Choice.

The evening also recognised special honourees Audrey Joe-Ezigbo, Dr Ibilola Amao, Elohor Aiboni, Olu Verheijen and Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan for their contributions and leadership across the industry.

Adding to the evening’s celebratory atmosphere, the Lord Urban Choir delivered a performance that provided a musical highlight for guests.

The 2026 WIEN Gala & Awards was more than an anniversary celebration. It was an opportunity to recognise the women shaping the energy industry, spotlight organisations advancing inclusion and introduce a framework for measuring the progress still needed.

Six years into its journey, WIEN is setting its sights on what comes next: a more inclusive energy sector where women’s participation, leadership and contributions are not simply acknowledged but reflected in measurable outcomes.

item.content:encoded:
The role of home appliances is changing. Today’s consumers expect more than products that simply perform everyday tasks. They want solutions that are intuitive, efficient and capable of making daily life easier. Across Africa, rapid urbanisation, changing lifestyles and growing digital adoption are reshaping consumer expectations. Homeowners are increasingly seeking appliances that combine convenience, performance, energy efficiency and intelligent functionality while fitting seamlessly into their everyday routines.

In response, LG Electronics continues to develop innovations that place people at the centre of technology. Guided by its vision for smarter, more connected living, the company is introducing solutions that help consumers spend less time on household chores and more time on what matters most.

Smarter Food Preservation for Modern Households

Food remains at the heart of every home, making efficient food storage and preservation a priority for many families. As households look for ways to keep groceries fresher for longer and reduce waste, refrigeration has become an essential part of modern living.

LG’s Side-by-Side Refrigerator is designed to meet these evolving needs by combining generous storage capacity with advanced cooling technologies that help maintain freshness for longer periods. Features such as Linear Cooling, DoorCooling+ and Multi-Air Flow systems on selected models help create a consistent cooling environment for everyday food items.

Its spacious design also offers greater storage flexibility and easier organisation, helping families manage groceries more conveniently while maximising available space. Beyond preserving food, the refrigerator reflects a growing consumer preference for appliances that deliver practical value while supporting a more organised and efficient lifestyle.

The Washing Machine That Understands Your Laundry

Laundry remains an essential household task, but caring for different fabric types can often be challenging. Consumers increasingly want solutions that simplify the process while protecting their clothes.

LG’s AI Direct Drive (AI DD) technology helps address this need through intelligent fabric care. By analysing laundry characteristics such as load weight and fabric softness, the system can determine suitable washing motions designed to deliver more effective and gentle cleaning performance.

Working alongside LG’s 6 Motion Direct Drive technology, AI DD helps provide a more tailored laundry experience while reducing the guesswork often associated with selecting wash settings.

Making Kitchen Clean-Up Easier with Smart Dish Care

As modern lifestyles become busier, consumers are increasingly looking for ways to reduce the time spent on repetitive household chores. Washing dishes after meals can often be one of the most time-consuming tasks in the home.

LG’s dishwasher solutions are designed to simplify this process through powerful cleaning performance and intelligent functionality that take the stress out of kitchen clean-up. Featuring technologies such as QuadWash on selected models, LG dishwashers use multi-directional spray arms to help ensure thorough cleaning from multiple angles, reaching areas that may be difficult to clean through traditional washing methods.

The result is a more convenient and hygienic dishwashing experience, allowing consumers to save time while maintaining high cleaning standards. For growing households and busy families, this translates into more time spent with loved ones and less time standing at the sink.

Advancing Connected Living Through LG ThinQ

Beyond individual appliances, LG continues to expand the possibilities of connected living through its LG ThinQ ecosystem. The platform allows compatible LG appliances to connect seamlessly, giving users greater visibility and control over their home environment through a smartphone. Depending on the appliance, users can monitor operations, access selected functions remotely and receive useful product insights.

This connected experience allows technology to work quietly in the background, helping consumers manage daily routines more efficiently while enjoying greater convenience and flexibility.

Innovation That Understands People

According to Oktai Kim, General Manager, Home Appliance Solutions, LG Electronics Nigeria, the future of home innovation lies in developing technologies that understand consumers and respond to their everyday needs.

“Consumers today want more than functionality. They are looking for appliances that simplify routines, save time, improve efficiency and fit naturally into their lifestyles. At LG, our focus is on creating innovations that deliver meaningful value and make everyday experiences better for our customers.”

He added: “Whether it is our Side-by-Side Refrigerators that help keep food fresher for longer, AI-powered washing machines that deliver intelligent fabric care, dishwasher solutions that simplify kitchen clean-up or connected home experiences through LG ThinQ, our goal remains the same: developing technologies that improve convenience and support better living for consumers across Africa.”

As consumer expectations continue to evolve, LG remains committed to creating products that move beyond traditional functionality to deliver experiences that are intuitive, connected and relevant to modern lifestyles.

By continuously developing solutions designed around real consumer needs, LG Electronics is helping shape a future where innovation is measured not only by what technology can do but also by how it improves everyday life.

item.title: Beyoncé Becomes First Artist in Grammy History to Earn 100 Nominations!
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Beyoncé has become the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations, landing a Best R&B Solo Performance nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" ahead of the 2027 Grammy Awards.

The post Beyoncé Becomes First Artist in Grammy History to Earn 100 Nominations! appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Beyoncé becomes the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram 

If you have ever wondered what triple digits look like on music’s biggest stage, Beyoncé just gave everyone the answer. The Houston-born global music superstar has officially become the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations, hitting the milestone with her latest nod for “Morning Dew (Donk)”, which is nominated for Best R&B Solo Performance at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards (2027 Grammys).

Released in July 2026 ahead of the 20th anniversary of her sophomore album B’Day, “Morning Dew (Donk)” puts her in a category alongside Kehlani, Victoria Monét, Jill Scott, and Nigerian star Tems. To put the 100-nomination milestone into perspective, no other recording artist has ever crossed into triple digits since the Grammys began. Beyoncé had previously been tied with her husband, Jay-Z, at 88 nominations each before breaking that tie in 2024 with 11 nods for Cowboy Carter to reach 99—and this latest recognition pushes her even further ahead as the artist with the highest number of Grammy nominations in history.

Beyoncé holding her three Grammy trophies at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards in 2025. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram 

It is also a good reminder of how long she has been doing this at the highest level. Beyoncé’s Grammy journey started all the way back in 2000 as part of Destiny’s Child with “Bills, Bills, Bills”, and across more than two decades as a solo artist, group member, and collaborator, she has built a record that keeps stretching further ahead of the pack.

Alongside holding the title for the most Grammy nominations of all time, she is already the most awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins, a record she first broke in 2023 when she surpassed late conductor Georg Solti’s 31 trophies. She pushed that tally even higher at the 2025 Grammys, taking home three awards—Album of the Year and Best Country Album for Cowboy Carter, as well as Best Country Duo/Group Performance for “II Most Wanted” alongside Miley Cyrus.

Now all eyes turn to Sunday, 7 February 2027, when the 2027 Grammy Awards take place at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles and we find out whether nomination number 100 turns into Grammy win number 36.

item.content:encoded:
Newlyweds Efya and Tomi Thomas at their white wedding reception in Accra. Photo Credit: Thret Studio/Instagram 

Two music stars, two countries, one beautiful love story! Nigerian singer Tomi Thomas and Ghanaian songstress Efya have made things official, celebrating their union in Accra with a wedding that brought Nigerian and Ghanaian traditions together. From their coordinated traditional looks to their elegant white wedding outfits and a song Tomi made especially for his bride, there was plenty to love about this celebration.

If you’ve followed the music scenes in Nigeria and Ghana, you’ll know that Tomi and Efya have each carved out their own place in contemporary African music. Tomi Thomas, who hails from Delta State, Nigeria, first gained recognition as part of the music collective L.O.S (Loud On Sound), before building a solo catalogue that moves across Afro-fusion and alternative sounds. Efya, born Jane Awindor in Kumasi, Ghana, is one of the country’s most celebrated vocalists, known for her soulful music and multiple Ghana Music Awards. Now, the two have added a beautiful new chapter to their story, bringing their families, friends and two cultures together in Accra.

Efya and Tomi Thomas in black and olive-green outfits for their wedding reception. Photo Credit: Photo Humor/Instagram 

One of the lovely fashion moments from the celebration was their Nigerian traditional attire. The couple coordinated in rich bronze-brown shades, with Tomi wearing a woven traditional robe, complete with a matching traditional cap. He accessorised with layered orange coral neck beads, matching wrist beads and black loafers, while carrying a circular feathered fan inscribed with “OGENEE”.

Efya was every bit his match in a fitted, floor-length bronze-brown gown, with gold and silver beadwork covering the corset bodice and sheer sleeves. The structured peplum details at the hips added shape to the dress, while a beaded treble clef motif on the skirt made a sweet reference to the music that brought so much of their story together. She finished with a pleated gold-and-bronze headwrap, a white-and-coral beaded choker, coral earrings and gold strappy heels.

Tomi Thomas and Efya in coordinated bronze-brown traditional attire for their wedding in Accra. Photo Credit: Tomi Thomas/Instagram 

For their white wedding, the couple opted for a timeless black-and-white palette. Tomi kept things classic in a double-breasted white tuxedo jacket, complete with a white pocket square, crisp dress shirt and black bow tie. Black tailored trousers and matching dress shoes completed his look. Efya, meanwhile, made a beautiful bridal entrance in a fitted white lace mermaid gown with an embellished illusion neckline, sheer floral lace long sleeves and a corset-style waist.

The voluminous detachable overskirt added another dimension to the dress, while her sleek low bun and large white structured bouquet with a jewelled centre completed her bridal look. Against a setting of chandeliers and warm floral installations, the newlyweds looked right at home.

Efya in her white lace mermaid gown and detachable overskirt for her wedding in Accra. Photo Credit: Thret Studios/Instagram

And because music is such a big part of their story, the celebration had a special musical detail too. Tomi shot the official music video for “Woman“, a song he made for his wife, featuring Ghanaian rapper M.anifest, on their wedding day. A song dedicated to his bride, filmed on the very day they became husband and wife? We think that’s a rather lovely way to mark the occasion. Between the cultural traditions, the beautiful outfit changes and the music woven into their celebration, Tomi Thomas and Efya gave us a wedding that was unmistakably theirs.
